newsitem.title: GERMANY: German soldiers club foreigners with baseball bats.
newsitem.headline: German soldiers club foreigners with baseball bats.

text.p: Shouting racist abuse, a gang of German soldiers armed with baseball bats and knives attacked three foreigners in western Germany, police said on Tuesday, prompting Defence Minister Volker Ruehe to order a special inquiry.

The nine soldiers, some of them masked and wearing German army uniforms, went on the rampage through the centre of the western town of Detmold late on Monday night and hunted down an Italian and two Turks, police said.
Some of the soldiers threatened to slit the Italian man's throat and clubbed their victims with the bats. The foreigners had to be treated in hospital for head injuries.
Police have detained nine young recruits in connection with the attack.

Defence Minister Ruehe issued a statement jointly with army spokesman Hartmut Bagger condemning "in the strongest terms" the attack, which also prompted a hail of condemnation from political parties and army organisations.
The attack came a day after Chancellor Helmut Kohl praised German soldiers for a spectacular operation on Friday in which they airlifted 120 German and other nationals out of Albania.
It came as a setback for Kohl's attempts to give the German army a normal status like that of any other country and show it had made a clean break with its Nazi past.
"The attacks are even more tragic because just a few days ago (German soldiers) risked their lives to rescue foreign citizens from the German embassy in Tirana," the joint statement said.

During the evacuation the soldiers opened fire, the first time German troops had done so under hostile conditions since World War Two, breaking a 50-year-old taboo on combat operations outside Germany.
The German army said the arrested men were aged between 20 and 23, came mainly from eastern Germany and had only been in the army for three weeks.

They had been part of Tank Reconnaissance Batallion 7 stationed at the Rommel Barracks some five km (three miles) from Detmold and were due to be trained as peacekeepers to be sent to Bosnia in the NATO-led SFOR force. A German army spokesman said they would no longer be on the training scheme.

"We have to act effectively and immediately to maintain confidence in the German armed forces, especially in the light of the high international respect they enjoy," Ruehe and Bagger said in the statement.
They said they regretted "this shameful behaviour of several German army troops towards foreign citizens" and would do everything in their power to punish the assailants and maintain army discipline.
Last night's attack came a week after the German parliament's armed forces ombudswoman Claire Marienfeld said in her annual report there were no organised extreme right-wing tendencies in the army.
Ruehe, standing by her report, told journalists the attack was an "isolated incident" and said the nine had been young recruits whose attitudes were not typical in the army.
"These are attitudes that developed during their 20 years in society and not their three months," said Ruehe, who issued a personal apology to the victims.

The president of the German Army Association, Juergen Meinberg, condemned the attacks saying that it was an "isolated case" and said steps should be taken to ensure the incident did not damage the German army's reputation.
Opposition Social Democrats defence spokesman in parliament Manfred Opel called for a fresh inquiry into right-wing extremism in the army.
